passage:
Dear Seema,
You asked why I stopped wearing the "lucky" green dupatta to the Sunday market. Here's the honest answer.
After three bad Sundays in a row, I sat down with a notebook and split a page in two. Left side: what I control. Recipes, fresh stock, a clear price board, being there on time, talking to customers. Right side: what I don't. Rain. A wedding in the next lane pulling the crowd away. Whatever mood people wake up in.
I put all my effort into the left side. New cardamom buns, a bigger board. The right side I let be. When it rained last week and I sold half, I didn't blame the dupatta, and I didn't blame myself.
Sales are better overall. Some Sundays are still bad. That's the right side of the page.
Your akka,
Leela

qa.q: What did Leela write on the right side of the page?
qa.a: Rain, a wedding in the next lane pulling the crowd away, and whatever mood people wake up in.

qa.q: How does Leela feel about the rainy week when she sold half?
qa.a: She seems calm and steady; she blames neither the dupatta nor herself, because she has accepted rain as outside her control. 🙂

qa.q: Which choice turned three bad Sundays into a plan?
qa.a: Splitting the page into what she controls and what she doesn't let Leela pour effort into recipes and the price board instead of a lucky dupatta.

qa.q: What might change for Seema if she tried Leela's two-sided page on one of Seema's own worries?
qa.a: Seema might stop spending energy on things out of reach and feel less guilty when luck goes the other way.

grounding: A young woman separates what she controls at her market stall from chance, dropping her lucky charm and her self-blame.

passage:
Thirty rejections, Gautam. That's the number people always ask me about. Honestly, I nearly didn't get through them. For months I blamed myself for every no, and I also started doing odd things: the same blue kurta, the same pen, left foot first into every office lobby.
Then my mother asked me something simple. "Jaya beti, which part of an interview is actually yours?" So I made two lists. Mine: preparation, my portfolio, practising answers aloud, a polite follow-up. Not mine: how many people applied, the panel's mood, whether a hiring freeze came in.
I dropped the kurta business and put those hours into mock interviews with friends. I still got rejections. But when one came, I asked: did I do my part? If yes, I let it go.
The first offer came in month seven.

qa.q: What did Jaya's mother ask her?
qa.a: "Jaya beti, which part of an interview is actually yours?"

qa.q: How did Jaya feel during the months she blamed herself for every no?
qa.a: She felt anxious and responsible for everything, which is why she grabbed at rituals like the blue kurta for a sense of control.

qa.q: What choice did Jaya make after writing the two lists?
qa.a: She dropped the kurta and pen rituals and put those hours into mock interviews, the part she actually controlled.

qa.q: How might Gautam's listeners who are facing their own rejections hear Jaya's story?
qa.a: They might feel relief that a no isn't always their fault, and take away a practical way to spend their effort.

grounding: A young woman sorts interview outcomes into what she controls and what she doesn't, and drops lucky rituals and self-blame.

passage:
I'm Jeevan, and I've waited tables at this restaurant for four years. I've watched a lot of cooks. Farzana, our head cook since March, is different, and I'm still working out how.
When the food festival judges came last month, Anirban in the kitchen insisted on wearing the apron he wore when we won two years ago, and said we'd win if nobody said the word "lose". Farzana let him, but she spent the week tasting the fish curry every hour, fixing the plating, drilling us on timing.
We came fourth. Anirban blamed the apron. Farzana read the judges' notes aloud, circled "too salty" beside one dish, and said, "That one's ours to fix. The judge who hates coconut, that's not."
I don't know what she felt inside; she didn't cry or rage. But the next morning she was testing the salt again, humming.

qa.q: What place did the restaurant come at the food festival?
qa.a: The restaurant came fourth.

qa.q: What does Farzana's humming the next morning suggest, though Jeevan can't be sure?
qa.a: It suggests she wasn't weighed down by self-blame; she had accepted the part that was luck and felt settled working on what she could fix.

qa.q: Which of Farzana's choices after the result is most useful?
qa.a: Reading the notes and separating "too salty", which she can fix, from a judge who dislikes coconut, which she can't, sent her effort to the right place.

qa.q: How might Anirban see the fourth place differently from Farzana?
qa.a: Anirban blames the apron and luck, so he may feel helpless, while Farzana sees one dish she can improve.

grounding: A waiter watches a young head cook put effort into what she can fix and accept a judge's taste as chance.

passage:
Week 1, Monday: With the design competition brief pinned above her desk, Sumedha, twenty-five, split a sheet in two. Mine: drawings, site visits, a practice pitch every evening. Not mine: the jury's taste, how many firms enter. Madhav offered his lucky brass ring. "Keep it," she said, smiling. "Wear it for your own entry."
Week 3, Thursday: Pitch day. The projector died on the second slide. Sumedha picked up the printed boards she had made for exactly this and finished on paper.
Week 5, Tuesday: The result came: shortlisted, not selected. She read the jury's two lines of feedback twice and wrote "sections unclear" under Mine. She did not think about the ring once.
Darshan asked if she was upset. "A bit. But I did my part properly. The rest was a draw."

qa.q: What did Sumedha write on her sheet after reading the jury's feedback?
qa.a: She wrote "sections unclear" under Mine.

qa.q: How does Sumedha feel about not being selected, and what shows it?
qa.a: She is a bit disappointed, as she admits, but calm, because she knows she did her part properly and sees the rest as a draw rather than her fault.

qa.q: Which choice in Week 1 made the later weeks easier for Sumedha?
qa.a: Splitting the sheet into what was hers and what was not; it pointed her effort at drawings and practice, helped her handle the dead projector, and let her accept the result without blame or charms.

qa.q: How might Madhav see Sumedha's refusal of his lucky ring?
qa.a: Madhav probably meant it kindly; her smiling refusal might surprise him and show him that she trusts her preparation more than a charm.

grounding: It shows a young woman sorting what she controls from what she does not, putting effort into her part and accepting the outcome without superstition or self-blame.

passage:
Deepak, you keep asking why your Kamala Bua has no lucky charm on her shop door. Sit, I'll tell you.
At twenty-four she opened her tailoring shop in Bhopal: one machine and a borrowed table. That first monsoon the lane flooded twice and hardly anyone came. Neighbours had advice: turn the door, change the shop's name, wear a lucky stone. I was so worried I was ready to pay for all of it.
She sat me down with a notebook. "Vikas bhai, I can control my stitching, my prices, finishing on time, and opening at nine every day. I can't control the rain."
So she did those four things like clockwork. On the empty flood days she cut patterns. By Diwali the whole lane knew her blouses fit. She never once called the flood her fault, and never blamed the door either.

qa.q: What four things did Kamala say she could control?
qa.a: Her stitching, her prices, finishing on time, and opening at nine every day.

qa.q: Why was Vikas ready to pay for the neighbours' remedies?
qa.a: Vikas was worried for his sister and wanted to do something, anything, that felt like it could stop the bad luck.

qa.q: What turning point shows Kamala's approach working?
qa.a: Using the empty flood days to cut patterns instead of blaming herself or the door; by Diwali the lane knew her blouses fit.

qa.q: How might Deepak see the missing lucky charm after hearing this story?
qa.a: Deepak may now see the bare shop door as Kamala's choice, and understand that steady effort on the parts you control can matter more than any ritual.

grounding: It shows a young woman separating what she can control from bad luck, investing effort there and accepting the rain without superstition or self-blame.

passage: Two days before the Christmas plant sale, a hailstorm shredded half of Elizabeth's poinsettias in the greenhouse at her small nursery near Shillong. Her assistant, Aparna, was close to tears. "Maybe it's bad luck from moving the pots last week." Elizabeth sat on an upturned crate and took out a notebook. "Let's split it. What did we control? The greenhouse roof, the watering, the prices, the stall. What didn't we control? The hail." She wrote two columns. The roof panels had been old; she would replace those this month. The rest was weather. "No bad luck from pots," she said gently. "And no blaming ourselves for the sky." They spent the next day potting up the surviving plants and making a sign: HAIL SURVIVORS, EXTRA TOUGH. They sold out by noon.

qa.q: What did the sign say?
qa.a: HAIL SURVIVORS, EXTRA TOUGH.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth seem to feel sitting on the crate?
qa.a: Elizabeth seemed calm and steady, disappointed but focused on sorting what she could and couldn't control.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth separate skill from luck?
qa.a: She wrote two columns, fixing the old roof panels she controlled and accepting the hail as weather, without superstition or self-blame.

qa.q: How was Aparna feeling after the storm?
qa.a: Aparna was close to tears and worried it was bad luck from moving the pots.

grounding: After a hailstorm, a young nursery owner separates what she controlled from what was chance, without superstition or self-blame.

passage: The rejection email arrived on a Tuesday evening in the Hyderabad flat. Vinita read it twice, then sat on the balcony with a cup of tea going cold. Her roommate Farida came out. "Was it the interview dress? You didn't wear your lucky blue one." Vinita smiled a little. "I thought about that too, for a second." Then she took out a notebook and drew a line down the page. On one side: things I controlled. My portfolio, my answers, how I prepared for the case question. On the other: things I didn't. How many people applied, what the panel wanted, whether someone inside was already lined up. She circled one item on the first side: "Case answer, too long." "That I can fix," she said. "The rest isn't a verdict on me." Then she drank the cold tea anyway.

qa.q: What item did Vinita circle?
qa.a: Case answer, too long.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling on the balcony before the notebook?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and flat, letting her tea go cold, and briefly wondered about the lucky dress.

qa.q: What method did Vinita use, and why does it help?
qa.a: Splitting what she controlled from what she didn't, then working on the one fixable item, so she improves without self-blame or superstition.

qa.q: Why might Farida have mentioned the lucky dress?
qa.a: Farida was probably trying to comfort Vinita by finding a simple reason for the rejection.

grounding: After a job rejection, a young woman separates what she controlled from chance and works only on what she can fix.

passage:
"We lost," said Pooja, dropping her file on the chamber table. "Six months of work."
Vidya, her senior, poured two cups of chai. "Tell me what happened, in two lists. What was in your hands?"
"The research. The arguments. The way I handled the witness."
"And what wasn't?"
"Which judge we got. The other side's surprise document. Whether the witness remembered things right."
"Now. On your list, what would you change?"
Pooja thought. "I'd have prepared the witness more on dates. That's on me."
"Good. And the judge?"
"Not on me."
"Right." Vidya handed her a cup. "So you work on witness prep. And you don't rely on your lucky pen next time, or blame yourself for the judge's mood."
Pooja laughed despite herself. "How did you know about the pen?"
"Everyone in this chamber has a pen."

qa.q: What would Pooja change about her own work?
qa.a: She would have prepared the witness more on dates.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when she dropped the file on the table?
qa.a: She felt deflated and disappointed after losing six months of work.

qa.q: How did Vidya help Pooja separate skill from luck?
qa.a: By asking for two lists, what was in Pooja's hands and what wasn't, so she works on witness prep and lets go of the judge and the lucky pen.

qa.q: What does Vidya's last line suggest about her own experience?
qa.a: Vidya has seen many lawyers lean on lucky charms, and she gently teases Pooja from experience.

grounding: A young lawyer, guided by her senior, sorts a lost case into what she controlled and what was chance, dropping superstition and self-blame.

passage: Last spring I had three final-round interviews in two weeks, and I'm writing down how I got through them because Farida asked. I'm Rukmini, a woman who used to blame herself for everything. Before each interview I drew two columns. What I control: my preparation, my examples, sleeping properly, arriving early. What I don't: the panel's mood, who else applied, whether they'd already chosen someone internal. I put all my effort into the first column. I practised answers out loud. I didn't wear my "lucky" earrings, and I didn't read my horoscope. When I didn't get the first job, I looked at the first column. Had I done my part? Yes. The rest was not mine to carry. I got the third job. I don't think I was luckier; I just kept working on what was mine.

qa.q: How many final-round interviews did Rukmini have in two weeks?
qa.a: Three final-round interviews.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when the first job went to someone else?
qa.a: Rukmini felt disappointed but calm, able to accept it without self-blame after checking that her own part had been done.

qa.q: Why is Rukmini's two-column method wise?
qa.a: It puts effort into what she controls and accepts the random rest without superstition or self-blame.

qa.q: How might Farida see Rukmini's story?
qa.a: Farida, who asked how Rukmini got through, may see that calm comes from separating effort from luck, not from being fearless.

grounding: A young professional describes separating what she controls from luck, working hard on her part and accepting the rest without superstition or self-blame.

passage:
Coach's note, state badminton trials, Sunday.
Ira lost her quarter-final 19–21 in the third game. A net cord shot fell on her side at 19–all. Last year, a loss like that sent her into a week of blaming herself, or blaming the hall, or buying a new lucky wristband.
Today was different. Afterwards she sat with me and made two lists, on her own. What she controlled: her serve under pressure (weak), her footwork in the third game (good), her decision to play safe at 18. What she didn't: the net cord, the lighting, the draw. "I'll work on the serve," she said. "The net cord was just luck."
No wristband talk. No self-blame. I've added extra serving practice to her plan for next week.
Irawati

qa.q: What was the score of Ira's third game?
qa.a: She lost her quarter-final 19–21 in the third game.

qa.q: How can you tell Ira felt steadier after this loss than last year?
qa.a: She calmly sorted what she controlled from what she didn't and called the net cord "just luck", with no self-blame or lucky wristband.

qa.q: What will change in Ira's training, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Extra serving practice, because the serve was the weak part she controls, while the net cord was random.

qa.q: How might Irawati, the coach, feel watching Ira make the lists on her own?
qa.a: Irawati seems pleased and proud, noting the change from last year's self-blame and superstition.

grounding: A coach's note shows a young athlete separating what she controlled from luck after a loss, working on her serve and accepting the net cord.

passage:
Friday night.
The monsoon failed again this year, and half my tomato crop at the farm dried up. I'm Mehak, and three years ago this would have broken me. I'd have said I was cursed, or tied a lemon to the gate like my neighbour does.
This time I sat with a notebook. What I controlled: I chose drought-tolerant seeds for half the field (those survived), I set up the drip lines, I kept records. What I didn't: the rain, the heat, the price at the mandi. Lalit bhaiya, who farms next to me, says I should do a puja for rain. I told him he can, and I'll join if he likes. But I also told him I'm switching the whole field to the tougher seeds next year and digging the second farm pond. That's mine to do. The rain isn't.

qa.q: What did Mehak choose for half the field?
qa.a: Drought-tolerant seeds for half the field.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling about the failed monsoon this time?
qa.a: Mehak felt disappointed but steady, not cursed or broken, because of looking calmly at what was and wasn't under Mehak's control.

qa.q: What are Mehak's plans for next year, and why are they wise?
qa.a: Switching the whole field to tougher seeds and digging a second pond, putting effort where Mehak has control instead of blaming luck.

qa.q: How does Lalit bhaiya seem to see the failed rain?
qa.a: Lalit bhaiya sees rain as something to pray for, and Mehak respects that while also acting on what can be controlled.

grounding: A young farmer's diary shows separating skill from luck, investing effort in what can be controlled and accepting the failed rain without superstition or self-blame.

passage:
Hail had flattened the eastern half of Disha's onion field in eleven minutes. The western half, under the neem trees, stood almost untouched.
Uma Kaki came over at dusk with a steel tumbler of tea. "Someone's eye fell on your field," she said. "Tie a lemon and chillies at the gate. And you planted on a Tuesday, what did you expect?"
Disha sipped the tea and walked the rows with her. "Kaki, the hail hit the whole taluka. Patil's farm too, and he planted on a Friday."
That night Disha wrote in her notebook under two headings. Mine: the seed I chose, the drip lines, selling early to the cooperative, asking the farm officer about the damage survey. Not mine: the sky.
She underlined the farm officer and set her alarm for five, to start clearing the eastern half.

qa.q: How long did the hail take to flatten the eastern half of the field?
qa.a: Hail flattened the eastern half of Disha's onion field in eleven minutes.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling as she wrote the two headings?
qa.a: Disha felt steady rather than guilty, sorting the loss into what she chose and what came from the sky.

qa.q: Why is Disha's two-heading list a good response to the hail?
qa.a: It puts effort where Disha has control, like seed, drip lines and selling early, and lets go of the sky without blaming a Tuesday or an evil eye.

qa.q: How might Uma Kaki see the hail?
qa.a: Uma Kaki sees it through custom, as an evil eye or a bad planting day, and offers tea and the lemon and chillies out of care.

grounding: Shows a young farmer separating what she controls from random hail, without superstition or self-blame.

passage:
The third rejection email arrived while Vera was waiting for the tram in Valencia. Thank you for your submission. We received over two thousand films.
Javier read it over her shoulder. "You should've worn your lucky scarf when you clicked submit."
She laughed, but only a little. For a second she had actually thought about the scarf.
That evening she drew a line down a page. Left side: the edit, the sound mix, the synopsis, where she sent it. Right side: two thousand films, the jury's taste, whatever else was in the programme that year.
"The sound in the cafe scene is muddy," she said. "That's on me. I'll redo it. The jury? Not on me."
Javier nodded. "And the scarf?"
"The scarf stays in the drawer." She opened the list of festivals closing next month and chose two.

qa.q: How many films did the festival say it received?
qa.a: The festival said it received over two thousand films.

qa.q: What was Vera feeling when the third rejection arrived?
qa.a: Vera felt disappointed and, for a moment, tempted to put it down to luck, even half-thinking about the lucky scarf.

qa.q: How does Vera's line down the page help?
qa.a: It separates what Vera controls, like the edit and the muddy sound, from the jury and the competition, so she fixes the sound and applies again without self-blame.

qa.q: How might Javier see Vera's plan?
qa.a: Javier seems relieved and supportive, joking about the scarf but glad to see Vera focus on the parts she can change.

grounding: Shows a young filmmaker separating the parts of a rejection she controls from chance, without superstition or self-blame.

passage: In the badminton club's changing room, Simran sat with her notebook after losing the qualifier 19-21 in the third game. The last point had been a net cord that rolled over onto her side. Siddharth dropped onto the bench beside her. "Change your racket. And those socks are cursed." Simran laughed but kept writing, in two columns. Things I control: my second serve (four went long), footwork to the back corner, sleep before matches. Things I don't: the net cord, the draw, the air drifting in the hall. "You're not even angry," Siddharth said. "I am, a bit. But I'm not going to blame my socks, or myself for a net cord." The next morning she booked an extra hour of serve practice with the coach, and wore the same socks.

qa.q: How many of Simran's second serves went long?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling after the net-cord loss?
qa.a: Simran was a bit angry and disappointed, but calm enough not to blame the socks or herself for the net cord.

qa.q: What does Simran's two-column list help her do?
qa.a: It separates what she can improve, like her second serve and footwork, from luck like the net cord, so she puts effort where it counts.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see the loss differently?
qa.a: Siddharth blames the racket and the "cursed" socks, treating luck as something to fix with superstition.

grounding: Shows a person separating what she controls from luck after a loss, putting effort there and accepting the rest without superstition or self-blame.
